title: Endpoint Resource Saturation and Crash Pattern Detection Across Platforms
shortTitle: Endpoint Resource Saturation and Crash Pattern Detection ...
summary: This strategy detects endpoint resource exhaustion and crash patterns across operating systems, covering T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service. The technique matters because availability loss on a workstation or server can halt a business process, and the alert is often the loudest but least understood one a security team receives, since the same symptoms come from faulty software, capacity shortfalls, and hardware faults. Detection depends on performance counters, crash and memory dump records, and the process or connection data that identifies what consumed the resource. The main failure is attribution: resource data alone proves impact but not intent, so the rule must join the saturation window with the responsible process tree or request source before it can be called malicious.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for computers that run out of the power they need to do their work. The resources are memory, processor time, disk space, and network capacity. When one of them runs out, programs slow down or stop completely. An attacker can cause this on purpose. The rule watches resource levels, crashes, and the process that used the resource.
beginner.whyItMatters: Denial of service is not only about very large network attacks. A single process can eat all the memory on a server. A flood of requests can fill a web service queue. The result is a service that stops working for real users. These events look like normal performance problems at first, so you need context to tell an attack from a fault.
howItWorks: Agents and the operating system report performance counters for processor, memory, disk, and network.
The detection builds a baseline for each host and each service over several weeks.
It raises a candidate when a counter leaves the baseline and stays there.
Crash and memory dump records are joined to confirm that a process failed.
The rule then names the process or the remote source that grew the fastest.
Planned maintenance and known batch windows are filtered before an alert is sent.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital waiting room with only one receptionist. Patients arrive at a steady rate, and she handles them comfortably. If twenty people arrive at once and each asks a long question, the queue stops moving. Nobody has broken the door or the desk. The service is simply full. Endpoint denial of service is that queue. The computer is the receptionist, and the requests are the patients.
takeaways: Resource exhaustion needs a baseline before it means anything.
Impact evidence is not intent evidence, so join the cause.
Noisy neighbours and faulty software look identical at first.

objectives: Identify the performance counters that reveal endpoint resource exhaustion.
Build per host baselines so that saturation alerts are meaningful.
Correlate a saturation window with the process or source responsible.
Distinguish deliberate exhaustion from capacity and software faults.
Define escalation steps that protect service availability first.
dataSources: Operating system performance counters for processor, memory, disk, and network utilisation
Windows event log records for application crashes and unexpected service termination
Linux kernel out of memory killer messages naming the terminated process
Endpoint agent process resource usage records with the owning account and parent process
Web or application server access logs recording request volume and response times
logic: The pattern is a sustained departure from a host's normal resource envelope that coincides with a crash, a service restart, or a request timeout. The fields that must be correlated are the counter name and value, the timestamp window, the process or remote address consuming the resource, the crash or termination record, and the account that owns the consuming process. The malicious case differs from the benign one by cause and concentration: a backup job or an antivirus scan raises disk and processor load across the whole maintenance window with a known parent process, whereas a single unexpected process growing without bound, a burst of requests from one source, or a sudden drop in free memory with no scheduled activity explains the exhaustion and not the calendar. The crash record is what turns a performance observation into a security relevant event.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Endpoint Resource Saturation Followed by Crash
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: performance_threshold
#     counter:
#       - 'memory_committed_percent'
#       - 'processor_time_percent'
#     value|gte: 95
#   crash:
#     event_type: application_crash
#   condition: selection and crash
# level: high
falsePositives: Month end batch processing that legitimately loads the database server
Backup windows that saturate disk input and output for an hour or more
Antivirus full scans that consume processor and memory across many hosts
A memory leak in an in house application after a long uptime
Legitimate traffic spikes during a product launch or a seasonal sale
tuningNotes: Exclude scheduled batch and backup windows by time and host group before you alert, because they account for most of the noise, and require a crash, a timeout, or a service restart inside the same window so that plain high utilisation stays quiet. Baseline per host class rather than globally, since a build server and a domain controller have very different normal ranges. Excluding those windows means a deliberate flood during a batch period is quieter, so keep a request rate rule on the public facing services that ignores the maintenance calendar.
